a:r.a:t: This slide shows the deployed architecture.

The data starts at the EIA API and is saved as a raw CSV snapshot. Then the training pipeline creates the model artifacts, including the XGBoost model and a compact SARIMA representation. Those files are packaged into the API container.

At runtime, the Flask API exposes endpoints such as /health, /metadata, and /predict. The Streamlit app is a separate Cloud Run service. It does not load the model directly. Instead, it sends a POST request to the Flask API and receives forecast JSON back.

I deployed the two services separately on Google Cloud Run. This was important for the course requirement, but it is also a better architecture. The UI can change without rebuilding the model API, and the API can be tested directly with tools like curl or Postman.

One challenge here was that SARIMA initially produced a very large model artifact. That made deployment slow and impractical, so I changed the storage approach to keep compact parameters instead of saving a huge fitted object. I also set the API memory to 1 GiB on Cloud Run so SARIMA forecasts would not cause the instance to terminate.
